sections.text:
The letter is addressed to foreigners. They are scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, and they are being insulted and treated as outsiders. Peter begins with a blessing, and the first thing he gives them is hope: God has caused them to be “born again to a living hope” through the resurrection of Jesus.

Then he tells them who they are. They are not nobodies. They are a chosen people, a holy nation, called “out of darkness into his marvelous light.” And so, as they live among their neighbors, they are to be known for good lives. They are to respect authorities and to bear unjust suffering the way Christ did, without paying back evil for evil. Of him Peter says, “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back.”

The letter is written to people who may feel they do not belong anywhere. It tells them they belong to God.

The letter presents itself as written by the apostle Peter from a place it calls Babylon, generally understood as Rome, with the help of Silvanus. It is usually dated to the early 60s. Some scholars think it was written later in his name. The readers lived in regions of what is now Turkey.

The passage about Christ preaching to the spirits in prison (3:19 and 20) is one of the most puzzling in the New Testament and has several explanations. The instructions to slaves and to wives are read with the same care as similar passages in Paul’s letters. The book’s teaching on suffering has sustained Christians under pressure in every century.
